title: underwater discoveries reveal ancient aboriginal landscape
dek: rising seas drowned more than two million square kilometres of australia's continental shelf, but the archaeological record survived beneath the waves.
body: divers found stone artefacts beneath the waves of the murujuga region in western australia. the finds came from two distinct spots: a former freshwater spring and a rocky hill overlooking an ancient river channel. these were not isolated discoveries but part of a wider cultural landscape now submerged beneath the sea.

researchers published the work in quaternary science reviews. the team included archaeologists from flinders university, the university of western australia, james cook university and the university of york, working alongside the murujuga aboriginal corporation. murujuga rangers received scientific diving training and took part in the underwater surveys, contributing directly to the identification and documentation of the material.

one site is linked to a freshwater spring, a vital resource for communities living in the region before the sea rose. the second sits near a rocky hill with a view over an ancient river channel. both places show how aboriginal people selected and used specific geographical features before they were inundated by rising waters after the last ice age.

analysis of the stone tools indicates some were made from raw material sourced near rosemary island, about 23 kilometres from where they were found. this suggests deliberate selection and transportation of stone across a landscape that now lies beneath the seabed. the distance implies planning and knowledge of the territory, even as the land disappeared under water.

the ngarda-ngarli people have cared for murujuga for at least 50,000 years. vincent adams, director of the murujuga aboriginal corporation, said the discoveries demonstrate the extent of the region's cultural landscape beyond its present-day coastline. what remains beneath the sea is an important part of their story, preserved beneath the waves.

the findings come after murujuga's inscription on the unesco world heritage list. researchers say the submerged sites highlight the importance of identifying and protecting archaeological heritage in underwater areas. each new discovery helps reveal another chapter of australia's deep human story, showing that these landscapes did not simply disappear when they were flooded.

louise brooke, a phd candidate at flinders university, emphasised the contribution of indigenous rangers to the research. their knowledge and connection to country were essential to investigating murujuga's submerged cultural landscapes. the study builds on earlier discoveries from 2020 and 2023 by the deep history of sea country project, which first identified evidence of aboriginal occupation on the submerged continental shelf.
doesnt_show: the exact age of the artefacts has not been determined; the study notes they may be considerably older than the 9,000-year flooding event
settle: radiocarbon dating of in situ organic material from the submerged sites would help establish a firm chronology
